episode.title: Vance Says Iran Conflict Isn’t a ‘War’; August Jobs in Focus
episode.description:
Today's top stories, with context, in just 15 minutes.
On today's podcast:
1) US Vice President JD Vance downplayed the scope of the conflict in Iran, saying he would not describe it as “a war” given major combat operations ended months ago — even after a brief resumption of military strikes earlier in the week.
2) Bloomberg Economics expects the unemployment rate to rise in August, and payroll gains to increase at a subpar pace. We see risks to our forecast tilted toward a higher unemployment rate and even lower payrolls.
3) Anthropic PBC is set to finalize an expansion of its revolving credit facility to $15 billion, according to people familiar with the matter, clearing a hurdle before the artificial intelligence firm’s public filing for its highly anticipated IPO.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: Karen, we begin with the latest from the Middle East. The war with Iran is now into its 6th month. Military strikes on both sides have intensified in recent days, but Vice President J.D. Vance is downplaying the scope of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a war right now. There is no active shooting. I recognize there is— there have been places where this has flared up. Major combat operations— again, major combat operations lasted for about 6 weeks.

utterances.speaker: B

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: The big question here really is how will the American public take these comments? Because you're left with 18 service members that were killed from the United States side. Of course, hundreds of others are injured. And then you've got 3,500 casualties on the Iranian side. But then the attempts or the remarks by J.D. Vance, of course, were seen as an effort to, to, to mild down the situation of this war in the Middle East effectively, because President Trump has been calling it a war. And this, of Of course, comes ahead of those midterm elections.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: In the meantime, Bloomberg's Zabeer Abu Omar says South Korea is reportedly preparing to send troops and a naval support ship to the Strait of Hormuz. That's according to local media reports that say President Trump is ramping up pressure on its Asian ally for not supporting the war.

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: Well, Nathan, the economic pressure is ramping up on the White House in the form of climbing gas prices. U.S. retail diesel rose to a record, threatening to further spike energy-driven inflation as wars in Iran and Russia roiled the market. The fuel climbed to a nationwide average of $5.85 a gallon above the former peak that was set in June 2022.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: And also on the economic front, Karen, stocks and treasuries are steady ahead of the August jobs report that could signal the path for interest rates, with odds of a September rate hike roughly even ahead of the numbers. Bloomberg's Michael McKee has a preview.

utterances.speaker: I
utterances.text: Absent any major surprise, the August employment report will be a predicate for next week's inflation numbers. Fed officials are fairly confident the labor market is at worst steady. Jobless claims are little changed, and surveys of manufacturing and service industries report companies are still hiring. While job growth is forecast to remain slow, the drop in the labor force driven by immigration policy has lowered the number of jobs that must be created to hold unemployment steady. And unemployment is forecast to have been unchanged last month. Average hourly earnings gains have slowed, and central bankers say that suggests there's no wage pressures on inflation. Michael McKee, Bloomberg Radio.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: All right, Mike, thanks. The BOJ could raise rates at 3 consecutive meetings through December in an extreme scenario where yen weakness persists, according to Nomura Securities.

And the credit facility would exceed the company's roughly $10 billion target.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: And the CEO of Anthropic's biggest rival, OpenAI, Sam Altman, says the industry has done a poor job communicating the benefits of artificial intelligence. Altman tells Bloomberg companies need to show how AI can give people more power and enable greater creativity.

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: I think the industry has done a terrible job of this on the whole. I think we have done a bad job ourselves, uh, you know, maybe better than some others, worse than some others. It is difficult, of course, to explain that this is, uh— the world should, in my opinion, should want us to worry a lot about this technology. The world should want us to think about all the ways that could go wrong, to talk about what we see coming, but not to sort of like stir up doom.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's comments come as research from Bloomberg Economics finds the benefits may already be showing up. It estimates U.S. labor productivity grew 3.1% in the year through the second quarter, compared with the official 2.5%. And that would be comparable to the late '90s tech boom.

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: Well, in Washington, Nathan, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to let the Postal Service enforce new rules for mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterm elections. The Justice Department filed an emergency request to lift a Boston federal judge's order blocking the Postal Service from mandating changes to how it handles election mail for the midterms. The Supreme Court announced a deadline of September 8th, Tuesday, for the Democratic state officials and voter advocacy groups that sued to file a response to the government's request.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: And on Capitol Hill, Karen, two Democratic congressmen are calling on the Department of Homeland Security to release millions of dollars in federal funding for a program aimed at protecting elections from cyberattacks. And we get that story from Bloomberg's Amy Morris in Washington.

utterances.speaker: J
utterances.text: Senator Alex Padilla of California and Representative Joe Morell of New York called on DHS to immediately release $39.6 million for the Election Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center and and other election security efforts included in the most recently enacted Homeland Security funding bill, which was signed into law in April. But the department has yet to spend that money. The congressman gave DHS until September 9th to give an update on the funding and its plans to hire staff to oversee election security. In Washington, Amy Morris, Bloomberg Radio.

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: All right, Amy, thanks. A note from the media world as it relates to elections: Fox News has fired anchor Maria Bartiromo effective immediately in what a company spokesperson called a quote, business decision. The newsletter Status reported that her dismissal was tied to a dispute at the news outlet over coverage of President Trump's speech in July, in which he shared claims about election interference. The newsletter says Fox asked correspondents not to report the claims. Bartiromo reportedly shared that information with the White House. Fox and Bartiromo did not respond to requests for comment. The president meanwhile wrote on social media, Maria is a, quote, total professional, and her fans will not be happy.

utterances.text: Good morning, I'm Nathan Hager. More than 6 months now into the war with Iran, Vice President JD Vance is saying he wouldn't call it a war now with major combat operations mostly at an end. That does not mean, he says though, that the U.S. isn't keeping the pressure on.

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: Economic pressure, military pressure, diplomatic pressure, covert pressure— of course these are things, these are tools in the president's toolkit.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: Well, that was Vice President JD Vance at a White House press briefing. And joining us this morning from Dubai is Bloomberg Middle East correspondent Abir Abu Omar. Abir, how does the pressure look in the region this morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: Good morning, Nathan. Well, I mean, if you're referring to the pressure on Iran, then it's real. It's, it's very much there, especially the economic pressure, right? The situation domestically in Iran when it comes to inflation levels, for example, we reported they were 80% higher year on year. Food inflation is also much higher than that. So the economic pressure is there. But the big question here is just how How much is it going to take for Iran to capitulate? Now, a lot of analysts do not think that the economic pressure campaign is going to be enough to do it, especially with the timelines that we're working with, Nathan, right? Because President Trump has until November, essentially, those looming midterm elections. Iran has said multiple times that it could withstand the economic pressure, the military pressure for months, if not years to come. And so it really comes back to the question of who's going to blink first. And at this point, our Bloomberg, Bloomberg Omic's team puts it best, probably. They say that, look, the entire Middle East right now is an arena for war and no one is really winning. There's no clear winner in sight, especially with what you're seeing happening in the Strait of Hormuz, because yes, it is right that a trickle of movement is there. We report that around 6 to 8 million barrels of oil on average are making their way through the Strait of Hormuz, so better than estimates before, but still nowhere near where it was pre-war. And of course, you're looking at the impact on all energy products, not just Brent crude and NY crude, but also diesel. US diesel in the United States is now at a record high, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: Yeah, that's true. Just crossed according to AAA, saying that it's about $5.85 a gallon heading into the final travel weekend here in the US for the Labor Day holiday. It makes you wonder whether economic and political pressure being felt on both sides at this point.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it's, it's that, that is probably what is going to come back to, right? Scott Bessant had laid out this economic pressure campaign against Iran weeks ago. And then we're starting to see a trickle of just how exactly it would look like. But then the big question is, is it going to really stop big oil buyers like China or India from purchasing Iranian oil? Now, we have to also understand that in the Strait of Hormuz, the US naval blockade, according to a lot of analysts that we speak to and ship owners, they say that it's quite successful at preventing Iranian crude products from coming out. But then again, the question here is how sustainable is that? How much money does it cost the United States to maintain this naval blockade and then eventually Iran is going to sell its oil, right, to China, to India. Just in a meeting at the beginning of this week in Kyrgyzstan, the Iranian president was meeting with some of his counterparts, and then we heard from some countries, including India, including China, their commitment to enhance trade ties with Iran. And so this is all still happening. And then, of course, the military pressure that started, or the military re-escalation in the region that started this week with President Trump saying that the initial strikes are against Iran for attempting to put mines in the Strait of Hormuz. And then Iran, of course, hitting countries in the region yet again, still contained compared to March. But this is a situation where no one really wins, neither economically nor physically.
